sentences: Against a dark background, a large white jar seems almost to float.
This is a Joseon moon jar, made of white porcelain.
It has no decoration at all; its broad, round body alone says everything.
Moon jars were made for roughly a century, from the late seventeenth century into the eighteenth.
Only about twenty large ones over 40 centimetres tall survive, and three of them are Korean National Treasures.
Start with the round mouth at the very top.
The short rim is a little wider than the foot below.
So the jar looks less like it is resting on the ground, and more like it is lifting gently off it.
A jar this large and round was too difficult to throw in one piece, so potters made the top and bottom halves separately, joined them, and fired them together.
Follow the seam running around the middle with your eyes.
The seam and slightly lopsided silhouette that result mean a moon jar shows a different face from every angle.
Compare the left and right shoulders slowly.
Because of this asymmetry, the outline changes with each step you take around it.
Now come closer to the surface.
Its white is not pure but a warm milky tone touched with grey.
Around the bright reflections you can watch the surface shift between milky and grey as the light changes.
Notice the yellowish stains here and there on the body.
On the moon jar that is a National Treasure at the Leeum Museum, similar stains were analysed.
They are thought to be vegetable oil, a sign the jar was used in daily life.
The foot is small and low compared with the swelling body.
A jar this big could easily crack or warp in the kiln, so perfect symmetry was never really within reach, right from the start.
Once simply called a large white jar, it was renamed after Korea's liberation.
Twentieth-century painters and art historians, notably Kim Whanki and Choi Sunu, popularized the name moon jar for its resemblance to a full moon.
Kim wrote of his fascination with it in 1949.
It became a symbol of Korean beauty, and in 2011 even its official treasure name changed to moon jar.
Choi Sunu compared it to a handsome daughter-in-law, and the British potter Bernard Leach drew inspiration from it.
What remains when ornament is stripped away is a generous calm.
This quiet understatement is why Joseon porcelain is treasured in museums around the world.
Standing before it now, what kind of moon do you see?
